title: R. SARAVANAN VS. PERIYAR UNIVERSITY REP BY ITS REGISTRAR

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1136
Page 1 of 27
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 4216 OF
2020)
R. SARAVANAN ...Appellant(s)
VERSUS
PERIYAR UNIVERSITY REP BY ITS REGISTRAR
& ORS. ...Respondent(s)
J U D G M E N T
SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR, J.
This Special Leave Petition has been filed against the judgment
of reversal and raises an important question of law as to the extent of
powers and jurisdiction of the High Court under Clause 15 of the Letters
Patent of Madras High Court. Putting it precisely, the question that falls
for consideration is whether the Letters Patent Bench can interfere with
the decision of writ Court exercising powers under Article 226 of the
Constitution of India, merely because it held a different view in the
matter.
2. Leave granted.
3. R. Saravanan, who was the Deputy Registrar of the Periyar
University, is aggrieved by the judgment delivered by a Division Bench

Page 2 of 27
of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in an intra-Court Appeal1
filed by the Periyar University by which the writ Court's order interfering
with the order of punishment has been set aside and the punishment of
removal from service awarded to the appellant has been restored.
4. The appellant was appointed on 2nd May 2000 on the substantive
post of Assistant Registrar by following due procedure for appointment
on the said post. While he was working as the Deputy Registrar, a
complaint regarding his assets was received in the Department of Higher
Education and the Registrar (I/c) of the Periyar University was directed
by a letter dated 4th June 2008 to conduct a departmental preliminary
inquiry. The letter dated 4th June 2008 was followed by further
directions to the Vice Chancellor, as contained in the letters dated 24th
December 2008 and 10th February 2009, to constitute an Inquiry
Committee to look into the allegations of amassing of wealth by the
appellant disproportionate to his known sources of income. The
appellant appeared before Three-member Committee so constituted
pursuant to the aforementioned directions and submitted his reply. It is
stated that the appellant who was holding the administrative charges in
the University threatened the Committee members and refused to
cooperate with the inquiry. Whereafter, the University constituted One-man Commission on 19th April 2011 to conduct an inquiry into the
allegations against the appellant. The Commission submitted a report
wherein a few charges against the appellant were held to be proved; of

Page 3 of 27
which three charges, namely, Charge Nos. 1, 4 and 10 are only relevant.
The allegation against the appellant under Charge No. 1 was that he
influenced the Authority to grant affiliation to Ganga College of
Education in which his wife was a Managing Trustee. The Charge No. 4
related to a house property at Periyar Nagar in the name of the
appellant's mother which was allegedly purchased by him without due
permission from the University. The appellant had a Santro car worth
Rs. 4 lakhs which he was alleged to have purchased beyond his regular
source of income and thus, committed a misconduct. This was Charge
No. 10.
5. By a communication dated 26th July 2013, the appellant was
informed that the report of One-man Commission was considered and
the findings thereof were accepted by the Syndicate which took a
decision to remove him from service with effect from 27th July 2013.
Aggrieved thereby, the appellant invoked jurisdiction of the High Court
under Article 226 of Constitution of India in W.P. No. 23936 of 2013 to
challenge the removal order dated 26th July 2013 with a prayer for his
reinstatement in service and consequential benefits.
6. The appellant contended that One-man Commission had no
authority to frame charges; it was constituted merely to verify the facts.
According to him, the inquiry conducted by One-man Commission was
without authority of law and the order of removal from service was void.
On the other hand, the Periyar University raised an objection to
maintainability of the writ petition on the ground that the appellant did

Page 4 of 27
not exhaust his statutory remedy of appeal under Rule 19 of the Tamil
Nadu Civil Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1955 (in short, T.N.
Service Rules) against the order of removal from service. The University
further contended that there was no bar in law to conduct the domestic
inquiry against the appellant through One-man Commission headed by
a retired Judicial Officer.
7. The writ Court examined the report of One-man Commission and
held that the findings recorded by the Commission were not based on
any material on record. The writ Court referred to the decisions in
"Bharat Iron Works v. Bhagubhai Balubhai Patel & Ors."
2 and "Rajinder
Kumar Kindra v. Delhi Administration through Secretary (Labour) &
Ors.
"3, wherein this Court has held that a finding recorded by the
Authority would be perverse if there is no evidence to support such
finding, and formed an opinion to interfere with the decision of the
University to impose the penalty of removal from service upon the
appellant. In the Writ Appeal filed under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent,
the Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Madras re-appreciated the materials produced in the domestic inquiry and came
to a conclusion that the report of One-man Commission is corroborated
by the documentary evidence produced by the Periyar University in
course of the inquiry against the appellant. Upon such a finding, the
Letters Patent Bench has interfered with the order passed by writ Court.

2 Bharat Iron Works v. Bhagubhai Balubhai Patel & Ors. : (1976) 1 SCC 518
3 Rajinder Kumar Kindra v. Delhi Administration through Secretary (Labour) & Ors. : (1984) 4 SCC 635

Page 5 of 27
8. The appellant who is a Government servant appointed on a
substantive post has a right to hold such post. He is protected under
Article 311 of the Constitution of India and he cannot be dismissed or
removed from service or reduced in rank by an authority subordinate to
the Appointing Authority. He is also protected against an order of
dismissal or removal from service or reduction in rank without being
heard. Therefore, a domestic inquiry is conducted against the
Government servant by supplying him written grounds of charge(s)
which is commonly known as memorandum of charges, if a major
penalty is proposed against him, and he is afforded a reasonable
opportunity to defend himself. True it is, that these Constitutional
safeguards are embedded in the statutory Rules applicable to the
employees of the University and the domestic inquiry against the
appellant was required to be conducted following the statutory Rules.
9. Clause (13) under Chapter VIII of the Statutes of the Periyar
University provides that the T.N. Service Rules shall apply to the
employees of the University. Under these Rules, the employee of the
University is required to be supplied a statement of allegations in the
domestic inquiry where it is proposed to impose a major penalty. The
employee of the University can file a written statement of defence and is
entitled to have a copy of the inquiry report. He shall be provided a
reasonable time, but ordinarily not exceeding one month, to show cause
against the findings recorded in the inquiry report. However, the
procedural requirements can be waived off in exceptional cases for
special and sufficient reasons to be recorded in writing, that there is

Page 6 of 27
difficulty in observing such requirements. The Rules further provide that
the Competent Authority may impose minor as well as major penalty
upon the employees of the University for good and sufficient reason.
This is a common ground that the memorandum of charges served upon
the appellant contained specific imputations of misconduct which were
required to be examined in a properly constituted domestic inquiry. The
appellant, however, contends that neither any disciplinary proceeding
was initiated nor was an Inquiry Officer appointed to look into the
allegations of misconduct committed by him and, that the proceedings
before One-man Commission were held in breach of the statutory Rules
and natural justice.
10. The rules of natural justice require a reasonable opportunity of
hearing to a Government servant before a decision is taken against him.
These rules presuppose that the administrative and quasi-judicial
inquiries are held in good faith and without bias. However, a complaint
regarding violation of the rules of natural justice must be examined on
the facts and circumstances of the case. There are different facets of
natural justice, all of which or some of which may not apply in every
case. It is, therefore, necessary to examine the nature of complaint and
the consequences thereof. Ultimately, it comes to whether any prejudice
has been caused to the Government servant on account of violation of
natural justice or breach of any procedural requirement under the
statutory Rules. However, every minor violation in observing the
procedural requirement shall not vitiate the inquiry or the punishment
imposed upon the delinquent employee, if it does not entail any

Page 7 of 27
prejudice to the Government servant. This Court has held on many
occasions that a distinction has to be drawn between the cases of
substantive violation and technical infringement of the rules of natural
justice (see "Viveka Nand Sethi v. Chairman, J&K Bank Ltd. & Ors."
4;
"State of U.P. v. Neeraj Awasthi & Ors."
5; "Mohd. Sartaj v. State of U.P. &
Ors."
6; "P.D. Agrawal v. State Bank of India & Ors."
7). It is also necessary
to examine whether the Government servant had clear and sufficient
knowledge of the proceedings against him and whether he participated
in the inquiry without any demur or whether by raising a technical
objection he is trying to make a mountain out of a molehill. There is also
considerable unanimity of judicial opinion that the Courts can, in
exercise of their discretion, refuse certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, or
injunction even where the facts are admitted or beyond dispute and
natural justice was not followed8. The case set up by the appellant before
the writ Court has to be examined keeping in mind the aforesaid
principles.
11. A memorandum of charges which contained imputations of
misconduct on fourteen counts was furnished to the appellant on 6th
June 2011 and he was given an opportunity to furnish his explanation.
The appellant denied the charges and raised an objection that relevant
documents relating to Charge Nos. 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11 and 12 were not

4 Viveka Nand Sethi v. Chairman, J&K Bank Ltd. & Ors. : (2005) 5 SCC 337
5
State of U.P. v. Neeraj Awasthi & Ors. : (2006) 1 SCC 667
6 Mohd. Sartaj v. State of U.P. & Ors. : (2006) 2 SCC 315
7 P.D. Agrawal v. State Bank of India & Ors. : (2006) 8 SCC 776
8 M.C. Mehta v. Union of India & Ors. : (1999) 6 SCC 237

Page 8 of 27
supplied to him. Later, two additional charges vide Charge Nos. 13 and
14 were also framed but those were excluded from consideration and
the punishment of removal from service is based on Charge Nos. 1, 4
and 10. The proceedings before One-man Commission were conducted
on several dates including on 29th April 2011, 16th May 2011, 6th June
2011, 4th July 2011, 1st August 2011, 29th August 2011 and 30th August
2011 and sufficient opportunity was given to the parties to lead
evidence. On behalf of the University, as many as 22 witnesses were
examined in presence of the appellant between 29th August 2011 and
4th June 2012. The inquiry report of One-man Commission held Charge
Nos. 1, 4, 10, 13 and 14 proved but the other charges were found not
proved and the appellant was given an opportunity to offer his
explanation as to the adverse findings recorded in the inquiry report.
Having regard to these facts, the question raised by the appellant on the
validity of domestic inquiry proceedings must be held untenable. We
hold that One-man Commission conducted the proceedings as per the
statutory Rules and the appellant had a clear understanding that he
was facing a disciplinary proceeding.
12. The challenge to formation of One-man Commission to inquire
into the charges against the appellant also must fail. Rule 17(g) of the
T.N. Service Rules provides that the Disciplinary Authority can appoint
an Authority to inquire into the charges against an employee of the
University. The Commission was headed by a retired Judicial Officer
and there is no dispute that he was appointed by the Competent
Authority. The Rules further provide that the charges may be framed by

Page 9 of 27
the Authorities directly higher to the delinquent Government servant
even if they are not the Competent Authority to impose the penalty, and
they may conduct the inquiry themselves or request the Competent
Authority to appoint an officer to conduct the inquiry. There is a specific
allegation against the appellant that he caused serious hindrances and
created an atmosphere of fear due to which Three-member Committee
could not proceed with the inquiry. Vide letter dated 19th April 2011, the
appellant was informed that One-man Commission has been
constituted and a memorandum of charges was served upon him. He
had clear knowledge of the imputations against him and he was afforded
full opportunity to put forth his defence. In response to the charges, he
tendered his explanation and participated in the proceedings before the
Commission. Even then, the constitution of One-man Commission was
challenged by the appellant in W.P. No. 12510 of 2012 on various
grounds wherein he agitated a specific grievance that the scope of
inquiry by One-man Commission was to ascertain facts and that no
departmental inquiry as per the Rules was conducted against him.
However, this writ petition was dismissed as infructuous by an order
dated 12th September 2017 and this order was never tested by the
appellant by filing a Writ Appeal in the High Court.
13. It was next contended that the findings recorded in the inquiry
report qua Charge Nos. 1, 4 and 10 were speculative and imaginary and
not based on any incriminating material against the appellant. The
witnesses who were examined in support of Charge No. 1 did not say
anything in relation to the charge of influencing the Authority to grant

Page 10 of 27
affiliation to Ganga College of Education where the appellant's wife was
a Managing Trustee. Except observing that the appellant was holding a
responsible position in the University, the Commission does not make a
reference to any incriminating material against the appellant.
Notwithstanding that, the Commission held the Charge No. 1 proved on
the ground that the appellant "could have" influenced the Authority for
granting affiliation to Ganga College of Education. The relevant portions
of the inquiry report by One-man Commission are extracted below:
"Since the deliquent (sic) was in the responsible position in the University,
influence of this position in the University granting affiliation for the Ganga
College during the year 2007 could not be ruled out. Hence the charge is
proved."
14. Charge No. 4 has been held proved on the ground that the
appellant failed to produce the title deed of the house property or any
other document to establish that his mother is bona fide owner of the
house in question. The Commission referred to Form 16 produced by
the appellant which indicated that he was paying monthly instalments
for the loan availed from HDFC Bank for construction of the said house.
The appellant was a co-loanee for the housing loan, but the Commission
observed that a co-loanee need not repay the loan unless he was 'the
principal loanee'. The inquiry report of One-man Commission has
discussed Charge No. 4 as under:
"The deliquent (sic) stated that the house belonged to her mother and he
was a co-obligant for the housing loan obtained for the construction of the house
from the HDFC Bank, Salem.
The deliquent (sic) also paid EMI regularly for the above loan from his
salary account and client (sic) exemption from Income Tax for the said EMI as
per Form 16 produced by him. The deliquent (sic) also confirmed the above fact
vide his petition dt. 23.04.2012 submitted to the Commission. The deliquent
(sic) also never obtained any permission for signing as Co-obligant in the loan

Page 11 of 27
papers from the University. Without being a genuine principle loanee one need
not repay the loan even in the capacity of Co-obligant.
The deliquent (sic) failed to produce the title deed of the property also and
other relevant documents to establish the fact that his mother is the bonafide
owner of the house.
Hence it is proved that he is the real owner of the property. Hence this
charge is proved."
15. Under Charge No. 10, the possession of Santro car has been held
to be a proved misconduct for the reason that the appellant did not
obtain permission from the University for purchase of the car or to avail
loan for that purpose. The conclusion of One-man Commission in the
inquiry report on Charge No. 10 is as under:
"The deliquent (sic) admitted that the possessed Santro Car TN45 Q 5705 and
for the purpose he got a loan of Rs.2,82,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs eighty two
thousand only) from the Centurion Bank, Coimbatore. He paid EMI Rs.6434/-
also regularly from his monthly salary income. The deliquent (sic) failed to
produce the permission obtained from the University for the purchase of the car
and for the loan obtained for the purpose. Hence the charge is proved."
16. The domestic inquiry against a government servant is in the
nature of a quasi-judicial proceeding. The inquiry is conducted to
ascertain substance in the allegations of misconduct. The role of an
Inquiry Officer in a domestic inquiry is to investigate the truth or
otherwise of the imputations of misconduct. The Inquiry Officer
discharges an important function and he is under a duty to follow the
Rules and to assess the materials dispassionately but the Inquiry Officer
does not assume the role of a prosecutor and it is not his duty to
somehow hold the charges proved. Naturally the Inquiry Officer is not
supposed to presume that the delinquent Government servant is guilty
of misconduct. On the contrary, his duty is confined to sifting the
evidence with a view to arrive at the truth.

Page 12 of 27
17. The report of the Inquiry Officer is the fundamental document
which may provide the departmental Authority a solid basis for coming
to a conclusion whether the charges framed against the Government
servant are proved or not, except in cases where the departmental
Authority differs with the findings recorded by the Inquiry Officer. The
inquiry report, therefore, assumes a great significance in the domestic
inquiry. The findings recorded in the inquiry report must be supported
by the materials on record. The Inquiry Officer while preparing his report
should rely only on the evidence adduced during the domestic inquiry
and he should not base his findings on mere conjectures and surmises.
The decision of the Inquiry Officer should be based upon a conclusion
that there is a preponderance of probability to hold the charges proved.
This is also a bounden duty of the Inquiry Officer to record a just and
reasonable decision. It is not necessary that there must be clear proof
in support of the allegations of misconduct and the Inquiry Officer would
be justified in recording a finding against the delinquent Government
servant if there is some evidence to support the charges. But then, a
finding not supported by any material on record must be held perverse.
It is one thing to say that the Inquiry Officer may consider even hearsay
evidence in the domestic inquiry, but it is not permissible in law that a
finding can be returned on mere assumptions, suppositions, surmises
and conjectures.
18. Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court exercises
plenary powers. The language used in Article 226 of the Constitution is

Page 13 of 27
very wide and the powers of the High Court extend to issue orders, writs
or directions including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus,
quo warranto, prohibition and certiorari as may be necessary for
enforcement of the fundamental rights and for other purposes as well.
The High Court may issue a certiorari in a case where there has been a
denial of natural justice or where a subordinate Tribunal is found to
have acted wholly without jurisdiction. The Constitution Bench
judgments in "Hari Vishnu Kamath v. Ahmad Ishaque & Ors."
9 and "The
Custodian of Evacuee v. Khan Saheb Abdul Shukoor"
10 firmly establish
the powers of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution to
issue a certiorari for correcting the errors of jurisdiction or where the
inferior Court or Tribunal acted with material irregularity. In "T.C.
Basappa v. T. Nagappa11" this Court held that a certiorari lies in all the
appropriate cases and is generally granted when a Court is seen to have
acted without or in excess of its jurisdiction. A decade thereafter, this
Court reiterated the same principles in "Syed Yakoob v. K. S.
Radhakrishnan"
12 and the law on the subject continues to be the same
even today. Speaking for the Constitution Bench, Mr. Justice P. B.
Gajendragadkar (as the learned Chief Justice then was) wrote the
following passage:
"The question about the limits of the jurisdiction of High Courts in
issuing a writ of certiorari under Art. 226 has been frequently considered by this
Court and the true legal position in that behalf is no longer in doubt. _A writ of
certiorari can be issued for correcting errors of jurisdiction committed by inferior
Courts or tribunals : these are cases where orders are passed by inferior Courts

9 Hari Vishnu Kamath v. Ahmad Ishaque & Ors. : AIR (1955) SC 233
10 The Custodian Of Evacuee v. Khan Saheb Abdul Shukoor : AIR (1961) SC 1089
11 T.C. Basappa v. T. Nagappa : AIR (1954) SC 440
12 Syed Yakoob v. K. S. Radhakrishnan : AIR (1964) SC 477

Page 14 of 27
or tribunals without jurisdiction, or is in excess of it, or as a result of failure to
exercise jurisdiction. A writ can similarly be issued where in exercise of
jurisdiction conferred on it, the Court or Tribunal acts illegally or improperly, as
for instance, it decides a question without giving an opportunity to be heard to
the party affected by the order, or where the procedure adopted in dealing with
the dispute is opposed to principles of natural justice. There is, however, no
doubt that the jurisdiction to issue a writ of certiorari is a supervisory
jurisdiction and the Court exercising it is not entitled to act as an appellate
Court. This limitation necessarily means that findings of fact reached by the
inferior Court or Tribunal as a result of the appreciation of evidence cannot be
reopened or questioned in writ proceedings. An error of law which is apparent
on the face of the record can be corrected by a writ, but not an error of fact,
however, grave it may appear to be. In regard to a finding of fact recorded by the
Tribunal, a writ of certiorari can be issued if it is shown that in recording the
said finding, the Tribunal had erroneously refused to admit admissible and
material evidence, or had erroneously admitted inadmissible evidence which has
influenced the impugned finding. Similarly, if a finding of fact is based on no
evidence, that would be regarded as an error of law which can be corrected by a
writ of certiorari." (emphasis supplied).
19. Any discussion on the powers of the writ Court is not complete
without referring to well-known limitations in law to issue writ. In "State
of Maharashtra v. Prabhu"
13 this Court held that the exercise of powers
by the writ Court should be for the sake of justice and the writ Court
may refrain from exercising its powers where interference with the order
under challenge may result in greater harm to the society. In "Ritesh
Tewari v. State of U.P." 14 this Court held that a writ can be issued only
in case of a grave miscarriage of justice or where there has been a
flagrant violation of law. The High Court should also refrain from
entering into the field of investigation which may be more appropriate
for a civil Court to do so in a properly instituted suit. True, the
jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution is not intended to
replace an ordinary remedy by way of a suit15. In "Mohammad Hanif v.
State of Assam"
16 this Court held that the writ remedy would not be

13 State of Maharashtra v. Prabhu : (1994) 2 SCC 481
14 Ritesh Tewari v. State of U.P. : (2010) 10 SCC 677
15 Mohan Pandey v. Ushal Rani Rajgaria (1992) 4 SCC 61
16 Mohammad Hanif v. State of Assam : (1969) 2 SCC 782

Page 15 of 27
appropriate in a case where the decision by the High Court may amount
to a decree declaring a party's title and the restoration of possession.
20. What follows from the aforementioned judicial precedents is that
the High Court may exercise its jurisdiction where there is an error
apparent on the face of record and such error has resulted in manifest
injustice to a party. What the inquiry report has unfolded is that the
appellant has been pronounced guilty without evidence. What could be
the worse kind of injustice to him than to hang him only on hearsay.
There is a complete lack of essential evidence to record a finding of guilt
against the appellant. The order of removal from service does not record
any reason why the Syndicate of the University accepted the report of
One-man Commission. The Disciplinary Authority by accepting the
report of One-man Commission completely overlooked that the findings
recorded thereunder are based on conjectures and surmises. The said
report draws inferences which legally cannot be held against the
appellant. The Disciplinary Authority while imposing punishment of
removal from service, without any legally admissible evidence, acted in
breach of natural justice. The writ Court was right in examining the
findings recorded in the report of One-man Commission to ascertain
whether to exercise the discretion under Article 226 of the Constitution.
Mr. Romy Chacko, the learned senior counsel for the Periyar University
would, however, contend that the writ Court cannot convert itself into a
Court of Appeal and examine for itself the correctness of the decision
taken by the departmental Authority. But this question does not arise
in this case because there is an appreciable difference between the

Page 16 of 27
appraisal of evidence and total lack of evidence3. It is well remembered
that a finding on perversity of a decision does not necessarily require a
re-appraisal of evidence. In the opinion of the writ Court, the decision
rendered in the domestic inquiry is perverse because there is no
concrete evidence at all to support the charge of misconduct. A decision
can also be labelled as perverse if the conclusion recorded in the
domestic inquiry defies logic or is such that no reasonable person can
arrive at a conclusion of guilt. Plainly speaking, if a decision on the face
of it is found to be based on conjectures and surmises or where a
decision is rendered by raising such inferences in law which are
impermissible, the writ Court is not denuded of its power to interfere in
the matter and remedy the injustice meted out to the Government
servant.
21. Therefore, a finding recorded by the Inquiry Officer not
supported by any evidence is open to challenge in a proceeding for
certiorari. It is then not a matter in the realm of appreciation of evidence
but really of recording a finding contrary to the materials on record. The
issue is a pure question of law and amenable to writ jurisdiction. A
certiorari may be granted where the statutory Authority acted without
or in excess of its jurisdiction, or in breach of natural justice, or contrary
to the applicable rules, or where the statutory Authority considered an
irrelevant fact or omitted a relevant fact, or where the decision taken by
the statutory Authority is hit by Wednesbury principle of
unreasonableness. The departmental Authority may be competent to

Page 17 of 27
enter upon an inquiry, but while making the inquiry it cannot act in
flagrant disregard to the fundamental principles of law. A decision based
on clear ignorance or disregard to the provisions of law or where there
is a manifest error apparent on the face of the record is certainly
amenable to a writ of certiorari.
22. There was one moment in the case when it was argued on behalf
of the University that the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution
filed by the appellant was not maintainable and the appellant was liable
to be relegated to alternate remedy of appeal under Rule 19 of the T.N.
Service Rules. This issue was not expressly decided by the writ Court
and the Division Bench also did not advert to this point. However, this
does not require a reference of any case law that the powers of writ Court
are not restricted by any fetters except for some self-imposed
restrictions. These powers are though discretionary, the High Court can
exercise its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution in
furtherance of justice, equity and good conscience. The powers of
judicial review are also exercised by the High Court to examine the
legality, irrationality or procedural impropriety in an order passed by
the departmental Authority. Sometimes it may be a sound exercise of
discretion to refuse to interfere with the order of the departmental
Authority because there is a legal remedy available to the Government
servant. But then, the rule of exhaustion of statutory remedy is a rule
of convenience and not a rule of rigid application. It is a self-imposed
limitation and does not create a bar or prohibition on exercise of the
powers by the writ Court. The award of punishment of dismissal or

Page 18 of 27
removal from service is the harshest measure of punishment and no less
than death penalty for the Government servant. It has cascading effects
and touches even the family of the employee. Such order of punishment
entails forfeiture of all service-linked benefits accrued to the
Government servant who is then rendered penniless. If such are the
drastic consequences, the writ Court should not be a mute spectator. In
appropriate cases, the writ Court is required to come out of the self-imposed bar and entertain the challenge laid to an order of punishment.
23. The writ Court held that the report of One-man Commission is
based on 'no evidence' and the charges against the appellant have been
found proved by raising impermissible inferences in law. Taking support
from the decision in "Delhi Cloth and General Mills Company v. Ludh
Budh Singh"
17, the writ Court held that it is the primary duty of the party
making allegations to establish the misconduct. But neither any
document was produced before One-man Commission nor was there
any evidence that the appellant influenced the Authority to grant
affiliation to Ganga College of Education. It further held that merely
because he was one of the signatories to the concerned file no inference
could have been drawn against the appellant that he influenced the
Authority. The charges framed for the possession of a house property
and for the purchase of Santro car were also held arbitrary and without
any basis. The writ Court, therefore, held that the findings recorded in
the inquiry report are without any factual basis or a foundation in law.
17 Delhi Cloth and General Mills Company v. Ludh Budh Singh : (1972) 1 SCC 595

Page 19 of 27
This is also a distinguishing feature of this case that the writ Court has
confined itself to the perversity of the findings recorded in the inquiry
report. However, the Letters Patent Bench reversed the findings
recorded by the writ Court on the ground that the materials on record
support the findings in the inquiry report. In doing so, the Letters Patent
Bench re-appreciated the entire material produced in the domestic
inquiry against the appellant which otherwise the Inquiry Officer or the
departmental Authority alone could have examined. On mere
conjectures, it held that the appellant had a vested interest in the
matter, he misused his official position, and manipulated and secured
affiliation to the college run by his wife. Contrary to the settled legal
position that the party making an allegation is required to lead evidence,
the Court raised an adverse inference against the appellant on the
ground that he did not produce the documents of title which could have
established ownership of the house property. It further held that the
appellant had assets disproportionate to his known sources of income
because he was paying monthly instalment for the house loan and also
for the purchase of vehicle, though he was earning only Rs. 29,175/-
per month.
24. The history of Letters Patent informs us that the establishment
of the High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras was necessitated
on account of uncertainty in the judicial administration during the East
India Company regime in India. The Regulating Act of 1773 empowered
the Crown by Charter to erect and establish a Supreme Court at Fort
William with full power and charge to exercise and perform all civil,

Page 20 of 27
criminal, admiralty and ecclesiastical jurisdictions in the Presidency
towns. On 26th March 1774, a Charter was issued by King George III
establishing a Court of Record, the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort
William in Bengal. Later, the Supreme Courts at Madras and Bombay
were established by King George II. Under the Government of India Act,
1858, all territories in India came to be governed directly by and in the
name of the Crown. Then came the Indian High Courts Act, 1861 (24-
25 Victoriae Reginae) which was passed on 6th August 1861 declaring it
lawful for Her Majesty, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal of United
Kingdom, to erect and establish a High Court of Judicature at Fort
William in Bengal and by like Letters Patent to erect and establish like
High Courts at Madras and Bombay. Under the Indian High Courts Act,
1861, it was provided under 9th Section that each of the High Courts
shall have and exercise, original as well as appellate, all such civil,
criminal, admiralty, vice-admiralty, testamentary, interstate and
matrimonial jurisdiction in the Presidency for which it was established.
It was further provided that the High Courts shall exercise all such
powers and authority for and in relation to the administration of justice
in the Presidency for which it was established as Her Majesty may by
such Letters Patent grant and direct, subject to limitations as may be
prescribed. Under 10th Section, it was provided that all jurisdictions
exercised by the Supreme Courts of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay over
the inhabitants of such parts of India shall be exercised by such High
Courts until the Crown otherwise provides.

25. A Letters Patent is a form of grant by the British Sovereign to the
patentee of some dignity, office, privilege, franchise or monopoly,
including monopoly rights in an invention.

commented on the nomenclature of Letters Patent and said that they
derive their name from the fact that they are not sealed up, but exposed

Patent of 26th June 1862 which constituted the High Court of Judicature
for the Presidency of Madras was replaced by the amended Charter of
High Court dated 28th December 1865. Clause 15 of the Letters Patent
of 1865 constituting the High Court of Judicature for the Presidency of
Madras provided an appeal from the Courts of original jurisdiction to
the High Court in its appellate jurisdiction, as under:
"15. Appeal from the Courts of original jurisdiction to the High Court in its

said High Court of Judicature at Madras from the judgment (not being a sentence
or order passed or made in any criminal trial) of one Judge of the said High

recited Act; and that an appeal shall also lie to the said High Court from the
judgment, not being a sentence or order as aforesaid, of two or more Judges of
the said High Court, or of such Division Court, wherever such Judges are equally
divided in opinion, and do not amount in number to a majority of the whole of
the Judges of the said High Court at the time being; but that the right of appeal
from other judgments of Judges of the said High Court, or of such Division Court,
shall be to Us, Our heirs or successors, in Our or their Privy Council, as
hereinafter provided."

powers of the appellate Court. It provides that an appeal shall lie to the
Division Bench under the Letters Patent from the judgment of Single
Judge of the High Court, except against the judgments prohibited by
Clause 15. That is to say, no appeal shall lie against the judgment of
Single Judge of the High Court passed in exercise of the appellate
jurisdiction in respect of a decree or order made in exercise of the
appellate jurisdiction by a Court subject to the superintendence of the
said High Court, and not being an order made in exercise of the
revisional jurisdiction, and not being a sentence or order passed or made
in exercise of power of superintendence under Section 107 of the
Government of India Act, 1919, or in exercise of the criminal
jurisdiction. There is unanimity of judicial opinions that the Letters

under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and therefore it cannot
be held that a Letters Patent appeal of this kind can only lie on a question
of law and not otherwise. The matter would have been different if the
Letters Patent appeal was from a decision of a learned Single Judge in a
second appeal to the High Court. In these circumstances it will be open

from a first appeal heard by a learned Single Judge, though generally
speaking the Letters Patent Bench would be slow to disturb concurrent
findings of fact of the two courts below. But there is no doubt that in an
appropriate case a Letters Patent Bench hearing an appeal from a learned
Single Judge of the High Court in a first appeal heard by him is entitled
to review even findings of fact. The contention of the appellant therefore
that the Letters Patent Bench was not in law entitled to reverse the
concurrent findings of fact must be negatived.""
28. However, the jurisdiction of the Letters Patent Bench to interfere
with the concurrent findings of fact should not be understood as if the
Letters Patent Bench can interfere in every matter because it is
exercising the powers of the appellate Court. The jurisdiction of the
Letters Patent Bench to examine a question of fact is not without fetters.
The Letters Patent Bench can be justified in reopening a question of fact
if it necessarily touches upon the merits of the case and is likely to have
a bearing on the decision in the case. It may be argued that the Letters
Patent Bench of the High Court is entitled to review findings of fact. But
what is necessary to keep in mind is that there is an inherent limitation
on exercise of powers by the appellate Bench. This is one of the well
settled legal principles that the appellate Court should not interfere with
the judgment of the Court of first instance unless a clear mistake which
will change the outcome of the case is found to have been committed by
the Court. The Letters Patent Bench should ordinarily be slow and
refrain from interfering with the discretion exercised by the writ Court
under Article 226 of the Constitution. A Letters Patent Bench sitting as
a Court of Correction exercises the same jurisdiction as is vested in the

Page 26 of 27
Single Judge but the Letters Patent Bench is required to give due weight
to the decision of the writ Court where it has exercised its discretion on
relevant considerations.
29. There may be different situations and the aggrieved party may
raise a host of grounds before the Letters Patent Bench. Some of the
grounds may be based on a question of law and the other may be just a
question of fact. The aggrieved party may also raise issues pertaining to
appreciation of evidence. But the Letters Patent Bench can interfere in
the matter only where the findings are demonstrably erroneous and the
mistake is glaring on the face of record. There must exist cogent grounds
and such grounds are not projected on some minor mistake in the
judgment under challenge. The Letters Patent Bench is not entitled to
interfere with the decision of writ Court on mere showing of some error
of fact or in law. If the decision rendered by the writ Court in exercise of
the powers under Article 226 of the Constitution is in furtherance of
justice, equity and good conscience and is not against public policy then
the Letters Patent Bench constituted under Clause 15 of the Letters
Patent of Madras High Court or similar provisions of the Letters Patent
of other High Courts cannot exercise its appellate jurisdiction under the
Letters Patent to interfere with the writ Court's decision. Simply put, the
Letters Patent Bench can not interfere with the decision rendered by the
writ Court which is otherwise just and reasonable.
